description: My goal: build an interactive 3D experience where students train like astronauts and run a Moon/Mars mission, making real trade-offs using NASA data on radiation, power, and life support. What I can do: full-stack development (React, Django, Three.js), game design, space education, and team leadership. Interests: astronaut training, space exploration, edtech, CanSat, and rocketry. Looking for: a 3D game developer, a space science researcher, and a pitch/video storyteller.
summary:
HOME BY SEVEN is a live-3D browser game that turns students aged 7–14 into junior astronauts. After a short training tutorial built on real astronaut skills (recycling oxygen, growing plants off-Earth, moving in low gravity and operating a robotic arm), the player launches for the Moon. A failure forces an emergency landing, and the mission becomes simple and urgent: you have seven days of resources to survive, repair and get home.

To do that, players run their own lunar outpost and balance four competing systems: life support, power, food production and radiation shielding. Every choice has a visible cost. Power sent to shielding during a solar storm is power the greenhouse does not get, so students experience real engineering trade-offs instead of memorizing facts.

Most space content for young learners is either oversimplified or too complex to hold their attention. HOME BY SEVEN closes that gap with a story children care about and science they can feel. It runs in the browser with no installation, so any school with a computer can use it.

Seven days. Four systems. One way home.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

HOME BY SEVEN is a live-3D web game in which a student aged 7–14 plays a junior astronaut who must survive seven days on the Moon and return to Earth. It is a mission trainer, not a quiz: the player learns by making the decisions a real crew would face.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Training. A short tutorial introduces four simplified astronaut skills: storing and recycling oxygen, growing plants off-Earth, working in low gravity, and operating an external robotic arm from inside the craft.

2. Launch and emergency. The flight to the Moon goes well until a failure forces a landing.

3. Seven days. The player runs a lunar outpost with limited supplies and balances four systems that compete for the same resources: life support, power, food production and radiation shielding. Improving one system costs another, and the player sees the consequence.

4. Return. If the crew is alive and the craft is ready by day seven, the player flies home. If not, they can try again with a different plan.

WHAT STUDENTS LEARN

Why gravity, atmosphere and radiation make the Moon dangerous, why oxygen, food and power depend on each other, and how to plan when resources are limited. Failure is part of the lesson.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Makes engineering trade-offs understandable for children without removing the science.

- Runs in a browser with no installation, so schools with basic computers can use it.

- Gives teachers a ready activity for lessons on space, physics and biology.

- Moves children from watching space to making decisions in it, and builds interest in STEM.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most outpost games are dashboards. HOME BY SEVEN is a story with a deadline and a personal goal: getting home. The world is live 3D instead of a flat panel, and the tutorial mirrors how real astronauts prepare before a mission.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Game and 3D: JavaScript and Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D in the browser, with React and Vite for the interface.

- Platform: runs on any laptop or school computer with a modern browser. No special hardware is needed.

- AI tools: Claude for planning, writing and coding support, and Higgsfield for the intro video. AI-generated video is marked with a visible watermark, and no NASA logos or mission identifiers appear in generated content.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age 7–14: short text, clear visuals, one decision at a time.

- Scientific validity: each mechanic is a simplified version of a real constraint, based on the NASA resources listed below.

- Realism over fantasy: no aliens and no invented technology.

- Access: web-based, no installation, playable on school hardware.
